newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Sweden budget leaks give glimpse of spending.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sweden budget leaks give glimpse of spending.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, seeking to salvage his political fortunes in the face of sinking opinion polls, is likely to reveal a moderately expansive budget next week.

Swedish media, in leaks common ahead of Swedish budgets, revealed on Wednesday that Persson in the April 15 spring budget will keep his promise to spend more money on elderly care, child care and schools.
Persson, while trying to honour his pledge to cut unemployment to four percent by the year 2000 from February's 8.8 percent, is walking a tightrope.
On the one hand he wants to placate voters who, sick of cuts to benefits, are fleeing his ruling Social Democratic party.

A survey by pollster Sifo in late March showed voter support for the minority government had fallen to 27.6 percent from 45 percent at the 1994 general election with conservative opposition, the Moderates, now with a clear lead in the polls.
On the other hand Persson does not want to damage investors' fragile confidence in Sweden, which could make interest rates soar and the crown's value plunge.
Finance Minister Erik Asbrink has tried to reassure market players, saying the money to be spent will not affect state finances, coming from an expected 1998 budget surplus.
The surplus was previously estimated at 10 billion crowns ($1.3 billion) but budget leaks said the government had raised its forecast to 12 billion crowns, the Swedish National Radio said.

Municipalities will get six billion crowns and regional authorities will receive two billion of the 10 billion Persson promised in extra measures for health care, elderly care and schools annually, a Centre Party source told Reuters.
The Centre Party is the government's informal partner in the seven party parliament and is involved in budget negotiations.
Economists said the leaks indicated the government would probably meet its budget targets and saw no shortterm risk of climbing bond yields.
However they were not impressed, saying the budget lacked longterm visions and the government was merely fighting to get reelected.
"Nothing of what I have seen will address the structural problems in the Swedish economy," said Olle Djerf, bank chief ecomomist at Nordbanken.
"It's just a matter of patching up the social welfare network and bring down unemployment by temporary measures."
Djerf called for big cuts in the amount employers have to pay to the state for each staff member, particularly in the service sector, to help boost growth and employment.

The April 15 budget proposal will offer an opportunity of early retirement while the unemployed will be allowed to work in health care, elderly care and child care with 90 percent of a regular salary, paid mostly by the government, the leaks showed.

Small companies will also be supported. Currently small companies pay five percent less in fees on staff with wages of less than 600,000 crowns and the government will propose to raise this to between 800,000 and 900,000, media said.
"It's good the government will raise the limit but it's not sufficient," said Knut Hallberg, Swedbank's senior economist.
Other measures include 15,000 new university places, a new trainee system, several large construction projects and lower electricity taxes for power intensive industries.
The government has also been forced to downscale its plans for large cutbacks on dental care expenses and will not cut back on personal assistants for the disabled, media said.
